title: Go home and tell (Mark 5:14–20)
hook: the healed man wants to follow, but Jesus sends him home to tell his own people
carry: tell the people who knew you

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man among the tombs who called himself Legion, met and set free. Your line was no one is too far.

The pig keepers run. Of course they do. They race into town and out to the farms, telling everyone what happened on the shore, and people come out to see. Here's what they find. The man they'd chained, the one who screamed all night in the hills, is sitting quietly next to Jesus, dressed, calm, himself again. You'd expect a party. Instead, Mark says, they were afraid. And they ask Jesus to leave. Then the healed man asks for what he wants most, and he's told to do something else.
screen: `THE PIG KEEPERS RUN.` → `THE TOWN COMES OUT.` → `THEY ASK HIM TO LEAVE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible, the town finds him "sitting, and clothed, and in his right mind: and they were afraid." Mark doesn't say exactly why. The herd is gone, and the people who saw it tell that part too. And a change this big can be frightening in itself. So they ask Jesus to go. As he's getting into the boat, the healed man begs to come too. You can understand it: this is the one person who didn't give up on him. Why would he stay among the people who chained him? But Jesus says no. "Go home to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had compassion on thee." That's a surprise in Mark. Remember the man with leprosy, on day one hundred sixty-two? Jesus told him to tell no one. Over and over in Mark, he tells people to keep quiet. Here, in Gentile country, he says the opposite: go and tell. And the man does. "And he departed, and began to publish in Decapolis how great things Jesus had done for him: and all men did marvel." Decapolis means ten cities, a region of Greek-speaking towns. Notice the small shift: Jesus told him to tell what the Lord had done; he tells what Jesus had done. Some readers see in that shift a hint of who Jesus is. And some call this man an early messenger to the Gentiles, sent before any apostle. His mission field wasn't far away. It was home, among the people who knew him at his worst.
screen: `SITTING, CLOTHED, IN HIS RIGHT MIND.` · `LET ME COME WITH YOU.` · `GO HOME TO THY FRIENDS.` · `TEN CITIES HEARD IT.`

segments.voice: Think back over the last month to one good thing that happened to you: a kindness someone did, a prayer that felt answered, if you pray, a day you got through that you weren't sure you would. Let it come back in detail. Then choose one person at home, or someone who knew you before, and imagine telling them, simply, what happened and who helped.
Decapolis, ten cities, the Greek-speaking region where Jesus sent the healed man home instead of letting him follow.
Your line: tell the people who knew you. Ten cities heard it from one man. Same time tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 177 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE HEM OF HIS GARMENT.`

howItsDone: Many Christians share their faith first with family and friends by telling what God has done in their own lives, a practice often called giving testimony.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: the narrator no longer states why the town was afraid (Mark 5:16 mentions the swine too); 'one of the first to carry the story' (a superlative) and 'many call' softened to 'an early messenger' and 'some'.
The 'messianic secret' contrast (1:44 vs. 5:19) is stated plainly; confirm.
Decapolis: a league of Hellenistic cities mostly east of the Jordan (Scythopolis lies west); confirm 'mostly east'.
'Lord' (5:19) vs. 'Jesus' (5:20) shift noted as something Christians often point to; confirm.
The man as 'one of the first to carry the story to the Gentiles' attributed to 'many'.
